text.p: Base metal prices remained softer during Friday afternoon LME trading, with the market generally under pressure from end-of-week profit-taking, traders said.

A sluggish performance in copper did not help, as the red metal showed little inclination to challenge Thursday's levels near $2,300 as nearby tightness evaporated. Despite a reasonable set of warehouse stock figures earlier, with most metals registering declines, the rest of the complex trended lower.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau Index ended 1.13 points higher at 239.15.

A sluggish performance in copper did not help, as the red metal showed little inclination to challenge Thursday's levels near $2,300 as nearby tightness evaporated. Despite a reasonable set of warehouse stock figures earlier, with most metals registering declines, the rest of the complex trended lower. Copper stocks rose 3,250 tonnes, which was much as expected. However, the main depressant on the market today was selling ahead of Third Wednesday pricing on Monday. Three months prices fell away from midsession onwards, and ended the session at $2,257, an $18 a tonne loss from Thursday.

Aluminium buckled under commission house sales and disappointed liquidation, with the 9,975-tonne stock draw not really impacting. Sentiment was not helped either by news that Norsk Hydro is to re-start 20,000 tonnes of idled capacity. Last business was at $1,564, down $12.
Profit-taking hit zinc after Thursday's run-up to new two-year highs, with last business at $1,210, down $12. Nickel was hurt by a 720-tonne stock increase and slid to finish at $7,740, down $140.
However, some consumer interest helped tin, which was steadier throughout and closed $35 higher at $5,975. Lead was dull, closing at an unchanged $656.
The alloy market was marked down to $1,470/75 a tonne.

CBOT wheat futures closed mixed, underpinned by optimism for a large sale of U.S. wheat this weekend to Pakistan and prospects for further sales of wheat to Asian customers, traders said. But Canadian logistical problems rattled the market. "The Pakistan tender is supporting it but the Canadian thing isn't
helping," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co. Wheat closed 1/2 cent per bushel higher to 1/4 lower, with March up 1/2 at $3.59-1/2.

CSCE world sugar futures ended firmer Friday amid steady options-linked buying, but a round of speculative liquidation knocked the market off its highs ahead of the close, dealers said. March closed up 0.14 cent at 10.78 cents after ranging from 10.61 to 10.86. Good fund buying was noted on second-position May, which gained 0.13 cent to close at 10.74.

New York precious metals futures extended this week's recovery Friday, led by commodity fund buying ahead of the US holiday weekend, traders said. COMEX and NYMEX metals trading ended about an hour earlier than usual Friday ahead of the US President's day holiday Monday which will close New York commodity exchanges. COMEX April gold ended up $3.70 an ounce at $346.70, after a push above Wednesday's high of $348.00 tripped buy stop orders which took the contract to an eight day intraday high at $348.60. Total estimated COMEX gold volume was 45,000
lots. In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $344.50/00, compared to the London Friday afternoon fix at $342.40 and the New York close Thursday around $340.75/25.

NYMEX gasoline hoisted oil prices to a higher end Friday amid anticipation of stronger gasoline demand while traders squared positions ahead of a long weekend. "We are sort of in between seasons right now, and, although the gasoline season has not kicked in, people are anticipating gasoline demand to rise after it has fallen so much," said John Bradberry, a dealer at
Transmontaigne Products Services Inc in Fayetville, Arkansas. March gasoline settled 1.07 cents a gallon higher at 64.25 cents while March crude ended up 39 cents a barrel at $22.41.
